policy_title: Introduce free personal social care and reform the care workforce
stated: Introduce free personal care, funded by £20bn per year, along the lines of the Scottish model, to ensure dignity in old age and for disabled people. Establish a career structure for carers with national pay, terms, and conditions, and reform the working visa system to end exploitation of overseas care workers.

source.quote: Elected Greens will bring together local authorities, trade unions and private providers to establish a career structure for carers, ensuring there is a pathway to progression that includes training and qualifications. This would have national pay, terms and conditions for all care workers and a proper workforce plan. Elected Greens will also change the working visa system to end the exploitation of overseas workers in the care sector. To address the social care crisis elected Greens will push for: • Increased pay rates and a career structure for carers to rebuild the care workforce. • Investment of £20bn per year. • Free personal care to ensure dignity in old age and for disabled people.

bearing_set.reason: Free personal care removes out-of-pocket social care costs and extends access, directly affecting social care adequacy and security in later life for older and disabled people.

Establishing a national career structure with set pay, terms, and conditions for carers, and reforming visa rules to end exploitation of overseas workers, directly affects pay levels, job quality, and employment rights for a large, historically low-paid workforce.
Free personal care reduces delayed hospital discharges (bed-blocking), which directly moves NHS waiting-list and A&E wait-time indicators — the social-care/NHS interface explicitly within O3 scope.

A stated funding commitment of £20bn/year is a material addition to public expenditure; with no funding source specified, it plausibly bears on debt-path sustainability and whether the spend is funded vs borrowed.

Currently, means-testing creates regressive wealth depletion for those just above asset thresholds; free personal care removes catastrophic care costs from individuals, narrowing the wealth gap between those who happen to need care and those who don't — a concrete O14 mechanism tied to the wealth-inequality indicator.

membership_note: Four fundamentals carry real verdicts: O8 (the design target — social care access and cost), O4 (explicit workforce pay and rights reform), O12 (£20bn/year uncommitted-source fiscal commitment), and O14 (removal of means-tested care-cost asset depletion narrows wealth inequality). O3 was considered (NHS/social care interface) but the effect is secondary and O8 is the primary home for social care. O2 was considered (removing care costs) but social care costs are an O8 indicator, not O2 essentials. O9 was considered for disabled people but the mechanism is service access, not anti-discrimination.
